description: Excommunication, the 1569 rebellion, three Catholic plots and the execution of Mary Queen of Scots.
content_html:
The Catholic Threat to Elizabeth

In the early years of her reign, Elizabeth adopted a policy of limited tolerance towards English Catholics. The Religious Settlement fined recusants but did not imprison them for their faith alone. However, from 1570 onwards the Catholic threat intensified significantly. A combination of papal action, foreign intervention and the presence of a rival claimant to the throne — Mary Queen of Scots — transformed the religious problem into an existential political crisis.

Excommunication, 1570

In February 1570, Pope Pius V issued the papal bull Regnans in Excelsis. This formally excommunicated Elizabeth — declared her a heretic and expelled her from the Catholic Church. More dangerously, it also released all Catholic subjects from their duty to obey her, effectively calling on Catholics to overthrow her. This transformed recusancy from a matter of personal religious conscience into a matter of political treason. Every Catholic who remained loyal to Rome could now be seen as a potential traitor.

Key Fact

Pope Pius V’s bull Regnans in Excelsis (1570) excommunicated Elizabeth and released Catholics from obedience to her. This made every Catholic potentially suspect of treason, hardened the government’s response to recusancy, and prompted the Ridolfi Plot of 1571.

The Northern Rebellion, 1569

The Northern Rebellion of 1569 (also known as the Rebellion of the Northern Earls) was the most serious internal military threat of Elizabeth’s reign. The earls of Northumberland and Westmorland led a force of approximately 5,000 men south from Durham, celebrating Catholic Mass and carrying banners of the Five Wounds of Christ — a symbol associated with the 1536 Pilgrimage of Grace. Their aims were to free Mary Queen of Scots, who had arrived in England in 1568 seeking refuge, and to restore Catholicism to England.

The rebellion collapsed without any significant battle. Queen Elizabeth moved Mary further south to prevent her rescue, the expected Spanish support from Philip II never materialised, and southern England did not rise in support. By February 1570, the earls had fled to Scotland. About 450 rebels were executed — a deliberately harsh response to deter future revolt. The collapse of the rebellion demonstrated Elizabeth’s firm control over most of England, but it also confirmed that the north remained a centre of Catholic sympathy.

The Three Catholic Plots

Between 1571 and 1586, three major Catholic plots threatened Elizabeth’s life. All three centred on plans to assassinate or depose Elizabeth and replace her with Mary Queen of Scots, supported by foreign Catholic powers.

Roberto Ridolfi was an Italian banker based in London who organised a plot in 1571 to assassinate Elizabeth, install Mary Queen of Scots as queen, and secure a Spanish invasion led by the Duke of Alva from the Netherlands. The English co-conspirator was the Duke of Norfolk — England’s leading Catholic nobleman, who had previously proposed marrying Mary. The plot was uncovered by Elizabeth’s intelligence network. Norfolk was executed in 1572. Elizabeth refused to execute Mary, despite Parliament’s demands, arguing that executing a fellow monarch would set a dangerous precedent.

The Throckmorton Plot of 1583 involved Francis Throckmorton, who was passing messages between Mary and the Spanish ambassador Bernadino de Mendoza, with a plan for a French Catholic army (led by the Duke of Guise) to invade England. Walsingham’s agents uncovered the plot; Throckmorton was tortured, confessed and executed in 1584. Mendoza was expelled from England.

The Babington Plot of 1586 was the most dangerous. Anthony Babington and a group of Catholic gentlemen planned to assassinate Elizabeth, free Mary from captivity and receive Spanish military support. Crucially, Walsingham’s agents had infiltrated the plot and were secretly reading all the letters exchanged between Babington and Mary. Mary’s letters included explicit approval of Elizabeth’s assassination — this was the evidence Walsingham needed. The conspirators were arrested and executed. Mary’s written approval of the plot finally gave Elizabeth and her Council the legal justification to put her on trial.

Mary Queen of Scots

Mary Stuart (1542–1587) was the daughter of James V of Scotland and Mary of Guise, and a granddaughter of Henry VIII’s sister Margaret Tudor. This lineage made her a credible claimant to the English throne, particularly in Catholic eyes, since they did not recognise Elizabeth’s legitimacy. Mary had been Queen of France and Queen of Scotland before being forced to abdicate in 1567. She fled to England in 1568 seeking Elizabeth’s protection — and found herself instead under house arrest, detained as a threat for nineteen years.

Despite repeated pressure from Parliament and her Council, Elizabeth was deeply reluctant to execute Mary. She argued that executing an anointed monarch was sacrilege and would set a precedent that could be used against herself. After the Babington Plot, however, the evidence was irrefutable: Mary had knowingly approved a plan to murder Elizabeth. Parliament passed the Bond of Association (1584), requiring signatories to hunt down and execute anyone in whose name a plot against Elizabeth was carried out. This was designed specifically to provide a legal basis for Mary’s death. Mary was put on trial, found guilty of treason and executed at Fotheringhay Castle on 8 February 1587.

Key Fact

Mary Queen of Scots was executed on 8 February 1587 at Fotheringhay Castle. The decisive evidence was her own letters, intercepted by Walsingham’s agents, in which she explicitly approved Anthony Babington’s plan to assassinate Elizabeth.
exam_tip_html: For questions about the Catholic threat, you need to know the three plots in order (Ridolfi 1571, Throckmorton 1583, Babington 1586) and their key features. For ‘Explain a cause’ questions, chain your reasoning: the Babington Plot was uncovered because Walsingham’s agents intercepted Mary’s letters → the letters showed she approved assassination → this gave the government the legal evidence needed to put her on trial. For 8-mark significance questions, address significance both at the time (the plots forced England into a more aggressive stance towards Catholicism) and over time (Mary’s execution changed the relationship with Spain and contributed to the 1588 Armada). Always use precise dates and names — vague references to ‘Catholic plots’ without specifics limit your marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Catholic threat intensified from 1570 when Pope Pius V’s bull Regnans in Excelsis excommunicated Elizabeth and released Catholics from obedience — turning recusancy into potential treason. The Northern Rebellion (1569) was the only armed uprising, and it collapsed quickly.
  • Three major plots threatened Elizabeth: the Ridolfi Plot (1571), the Throckmorton Plot (1583) and the Babington Plot (1586). All aimed to assassinate Elizabeth and replace her with Mary Queen of Scots. All were uncovered by Walsingham’s intelligence network.
  • Mary Queen of Scots was executed on 8 February 1587 after her letters approving the Babington Plot were intercepted. Her death removed the main focus of Catholic conspiracy but contributed to Philip II’s decision to launch the Armada in 1588.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Northern Rebellion of 1569.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: a precise feature with detail, e.g. the earls of Northumberland and Westmorland led approximately 5,000 men south, carrying banners of the Five Wounds of Christ, intending to free Mary Queen of Scots (2 marks). Emerging: a vague feature (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Babington Plot (1586).
practice_questions.marks: For each feature: Mastering: precise feature with accurate detail (2 marks). Emerging: simple feature without development (1 mark). Features may include: Anthony Babington planned to assassinate Elizabeth; the plot involved freeing Mary Queen of Scots; Spanish military support was expected; Walsingham's agents intercepted the letters; Mary approved the assassination in writing; the conspirators were arrested and executed. Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the papal bull Regnans in Excelsis (1570) for English Catholics.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a detailed chain with evidence, e.g. the bull excommunicated Elizabeth and released Catholics from obedience — this made every Catholic's loyalty suspect and prompted the government to take a much harder line on recusancy, increasing fines and eventually introducing the death penalty for harbouring Catholic priests. Secure: clear consequence with supporting evidence. Developing: relevant consequence with limited development. Emerging: a simple point. Maximum 6 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the execution of Mary Queen of Scots (1587) for the security of Elizabeth's reign.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained analysis of significance at the time (removed the main Catholic claimant; eliminated the focus of conspiracies; set a precedent for executing a monarch) AND over time (contributed to Philip II's decision to launch the Armada in 1588; confirmed Protestant succession). Secure: clear explanation with specific evidence. Developing: some explanation. Emerging: simple descriptive points. Maximum 8 marks.

practice_questions.text: How useful is a government report on the Babington Plot (1586) written by Francis Walsingham for understanding the Catholic threat to Elizabeth?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: integrates content (what the report reveals about the plot), provenance (Walsingham — the spymaster who uncovered the plot; likely to exaggerate threat to justify harsh response) and contextual knowledge (the plot was real; Mary's letters were genuine; but Walsingham's network may have entrapped plotters) to give a substantiated judgement. Secure: addresses two elements. Developing: mainly describes source. Emerging: simple comment. Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: 'The execution of Mary Queen of Scots in 1587 solved the Catholic threat to Elizabeth I.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: argues for (removed main claimant; eliminated focus of plots; no major Catholic conspiracy after 1587) AND against (provoked the Spanish Armada; Catholic missionary priests continued to operate; recusancy survived; Spain remained a threat) before a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: both sides with evidence and conclusion. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: simple. Maximum 12 marks.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the papal bull Regnans in Excelsis (1570) do?
flashcard_questions.a: Excommunicated Elizabeth and released Catholics from their duty to obey her.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Northern Rebellion and who led it?
flashcard_questions.a: 1569; the earls of Northumberland and Westmorland.

flashcard_questions.q: What were the aims of the Northern Rebellion?
flashcard_questions.a: To free Mary Queen of Scots and restore Catholicism to England.
Roberto Ridolfi, an Italian banker, with the Duke of Norfolk as the English co-conspirator.
A plan by Francis Throckmorton and the Spanish ambassador to assassinate Elizabeth and land a French army in England.

flashcard_questions.q: How was the Babington Plot (1586) uncovered?
flashcard_questions.a: Walsingham's agents intercepted and read letters between Babington and Mary Queen of Scots.

flashcard_questions.q: What decisive evidence justified Mary Queen of Scots' trial?
flashcard_questions.a: Her own letters explicitly approving Babington's plan to assassinate Elizabeth.

flashcard_questions.q: When and where was Mary Queen of Scots executed?
Why was Elizabeth reluctant to execute Mary Queen of Scots?
flashcard_questions.a: She believed executing an anointed monarch was sacrilege and could set a dangerous precedent.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Bond of Association (1584)?
flashcard_questions.a: A pledge to hunt down and execute anyone in whose name a plot against Elizabeth was carried out.

flashcard_questions.q: Why was Mary Queen of Scots a threat to Elizabeth from 1568?
flashcard_questions.a: She was a Catholic claimant to the English throne and became the focus of Catholic conspiracies.

flashcard_questions.q: The Northern Rebellion collapsed without significant battle. What was Elizabeth's response?
flashcard_questions.a: About 450 rebels were executed as a deliberate deterrent against future revolt.

glossary_terms.definition: The papal bull issued in 1570 by Pope Pius V that excommunicated Elizabeth I and theoretically released all Catholics from their duty to obey her.
The 1569 uprising led by the earls of Northumberland and Westmorland, intending to free Mary Queen of Scots and restore Catholicism to England.
A 1583 conspiracy organised by Francis Throckmorton, working with the Spanish ambassador, to assassinate Elizabeth and place Mary Queen of Scots on the throne.
A 1586 conspiracy in which Anthony Babington planned to assassinate Elizabeth and free Mary Queen of Scots, with Spanish military support.
